newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish government rejects talks with ETA again.
newsitem.headline: Spanish government rejects talks with ETA again.

text.p: Spain's government rejected on Tuesday an initiative by its moderate Basque allies to open a dialogue with the Basque separatist group ETA amid escalating tensions, saying talks would only fuel violence.

The Basque National Party (PNV), a nationalist but non-violent party backing the ruling Popular Party in parliament, asked the government on Monday to negotiate an end to violence plaguing the northern Basque region.
The PNV unveiled its proposal in a new document the morning after a powerful car bomb blew up in the Basque city of San Sebastian and days after a bicycle merchant was shot dead in the same city.
The government blamed ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) for both attacks.

"There are no short cuts in the war against terrorism," Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja said in a radio interview on Tuesday. "A hasty dialogue would only provide an oxygen balloon for the terrorists," he said.

The PNV, with five of 350 seats in parliament, has traditionally advocated negotiations with ETA. Its support in parliament is not essential to the Popular Party's majority but it does bolster the government in key votes.
The conservative government, headed by Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, has repeatedly rejected overtures for talks with ETA until the group renounces violence and lays down its arms.
The latest attacks only hardened its opposition to talks.
"It is very difficult to give credibility to a dialogue with those who hold two people hostage, after they killed a person and set off a car bomb," Mayor Oreja said.
Other major political parties also rejected the PNV's initiative, saying it was poorly timed, unclear and would only fan violence.

"At times like these one must maintain a cool head. But the nationalists start to consider the possibility of co-existence (with ETA) in the Basque country," said Basque Socialist leader Ramon Jauregui. "This mindset is very dangerous because it demonstrates violence pays off."
After last week's killing, government officials said ETA was trying to terrorise the Basque population, most of whom do not support the violent campaign for an independent state.
Though Sunday's car bomb caused no injuries, it damaged businesses and sent a new wave of fear through the region.
Last month, a woman shot dead an army officer in Madrid, another attack in which ETA was suspected. Street violence in Basque country has been on the rise since the beginning of the year.
Youths who sympathise with ETA rampage almost daily in northern cities and towns, burning cars, banks, public property and other targets seen as symbols of Spain's authority.

The resurgence of violence this year followed a relative lull in 1996 which had raised peace hopes. Officials said ETA killed five people last year, the lowest number since it began its campaign for independence in 1968.
